title: The prophets, looking back
hook: justice like a river, and a God who won't forget
tomorrow: who hears 'great joy' first in Luke? not who you'd guess.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Psalms: a song from a cave, and a book that lets every feeling reach God. Pray what you feel. Now, a strange word about singing.
screen: `PRAY WHAT YOU FEEL.` → `A STRANGE WORD ABOUT SINGING.`

segments.voice: The worship night was incredible: lights low, phones in the air, the bridge sung three times through. Now an odd verse. In the book of Amos, God says to people at worship: “Take thou away from me the noise of thy songs; for I will not hear the melody of thy viols.” Noise. Their best music, called noise. Why would God ever tell a choir to stop singing?
screen: `LIGHTS LOW, PHONES UP.` → `THE NOISE OF THY SONGS.` → `WHY TELL A CHOIR TO STOP?`

segments.voice: Read around the verse, and the puzzle solves itself. Amos was a herdsman from Tekoa who said he was no prophet, and no prophet's son. He spoke to people whose songs were rising while, in his words, their treading was upon the poor. The singing wasn't the problem. The singing was covering for something. So the very next line says what God wants instead: “But let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream.” Not a trickle on a feast day. A river that keeps coming. Micah folds it into one sentence: “what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?” Looking back, the prophets aren't fortune tellers. They're truth tellers to their own day, about the widow, the orphan, the poor and the stranger. And they don't only warn. Isaiah says a mother may forget her nursing child, “yet will I not forget thee.” Malachi asks the question underneath it all: “Have we not all one father? hath not one God created us?” If one God made everyone, the stranger at the gate is family. Something to repeat at dinner: Martin Luther King Jr. reached for Amos's river line in his speeches. Jews and Christians both read these books as scripture, and Christians also hear them pointing toward Jesus.
screen: `THE NOISE OF THY SONGS?` · `SONGS COVERING FOR SOMETHING.` · `JUDGMENT RUN DOWN AS WATERS.` · `HAVE WE NOT ALL ONE FATHER?` · then, large: `JUSTICE AND MERCY.`

segments.voice: A small plan for doing justice. Name one thing near you that isn't fair and is yours to touch: a chore always left to the same person, a friend who keeps getting talked over, money you owe. Then name what usually stops you, and one plain step past it, small enough for this week. If you pray, hold that step up with Micah's words: do justly, love mercy, walk humbly.
The prophets. Amos, Micah, Isaiah, Malachi and others: truth tellers who asked for justice like a river, and spoke of a God who won't forget.
Hold onto this: justice and mercy, side by side in one sentence of Micah's. A river, not a trickle.

howItsDone: Christians read the prophets in worship, especially in Advent, and some churches turn their words into work for the poor and the stranger; Jews read the prophets in the synagogue alongside the Torah.

fork.setup: your youth group is raising money for a new sound system. down the street, the food pantry is short on volunteers this month. what would Amos ask first?
options: drop the sound system; God doesn't want music.
keep the songs, and keep the river of justice moving too.
the music is worship, so it comes before everything else.
fork.reveal: Amos's problem wasn't the music; it was music covering for trampling the poor. let judgment run down as waters, and the songs ring true.

original.note: Hebrew: justice, setting things right. the word behind 'judgment' in Amos 5:24.

trapdoor: what you thought: prophets predicted the far future.
what it means: truth tellers who called their own day back to justice and mercy.
what a scholar hears: the KJV's 'judgment' in Amos 5:24 renders mishpat, justice; Amos 7:14 has him deny being a prophet or a prophet's son.
guess: truth tellers who called people to justice and mercy
fortune tellers who mainly predicted the far future

chat.says: rehearsal ran late and we left mr. dale the risers and all our trash. AGAIN. we sounded amazing tho
options: Amos would say the song isn't the whole thing. Ask the choir to stay and clean up.
Sounding amazing is what matters; Mr. Dale gets paid to clean up after events.
Feel bad about it, but it's not your job, so don't make it a big thing.
chat.meaning: In Amos the songs rose while people were trampled. Justice like a river means the music and how we treat Mr. Dale go together.

Unity thread (small): Malachi 2:10, 'Have we not all one father? hath not one God created us?', followed by 'if one God made everyone, the stranger at the gate is family' (the lesson's gloss, not the text's words). Confirm framing.
Amos 7:14 ('I was no prophet, neither was I a prophet's son') and Amos 5:11 ('your treading is upon the poor') paraphrased. Confirm.
Isaiah 49:15: 'a mother may forget her nursing child' paraphrases the KJV 'Can a woman forget her sucking child'; only 'yet will I not forget thee' is quoted.
Repeatable fact: Martin Luther King Jr. quoted Amos 5:24 in speeches (notably 'I Have a Dream', 1963); the lesson gives no date. Confirm.
Grace storyline: rehearsals for the senior concert run late and the choir leaves the custodian, Mr. Dale, to clean up (an ordinary person).
